item.title: OrBit (Re)turns: Tracking an open-source Linux rootkit across four years of forks and deployments
item.description:
Four-year evolution of OrBit Linux rootkit reveals it's a fork of open-source Medusa toolkit, deployed by state-sponsored UNC3886, eCrime BLOCKADE SPIDER, and RHOMBUS botnet operators.
Deep technical breakdown of OrBit's development reveals sophisticated operator tradecraft:
• **Two parallel lineages identified**: Full-featured "Lineage A" (66+ exports, PAM harvesting, network hiding) and lite "Lineage B" (54 exports, reduced footprint for specific environments)
• **Source attribution confirmed**: OrBit samples contain unstripped symbols (rkld.c, rknet.c, rkload.c) matching Medusa GitHub repo structure exactly. XOR obfuscation scheme (keys 0xA2/0xAA) and build pipeline artifacts prove common origin
• **Multi-actor deployment spanning 2022-2026**: UNC3886 🇨🇳 state espionage (VMware/Juniper infrastructure), BLOCKADE SPIDER eCrime (Embargo ransomware), and RHOMBUS botnet operations with C2 at cf0[.]pw resolving to Russian 🇷🇺 infrastructure
• **2025 capability expansion**: New pam_sm_authenticate hook enables service-side PAM impersonation, two-stage infector architecture adds C2 communication via cron jobs, breaking from purely passive SSH backdoor model
• **Persistence mechanisms**: LD_PRELOAD via patched ld.so, installs to /lib/libseconf/, /lib/locate/, or /lib64/libseconf/ with hidden credential storage in sshpass.txt/sshpass2.txt
Hunt for XOR-decoded string tables in .

item.title: Investigating server compromises with cgroups: A Linux DFIR primer
item.description:
New Linux DFIR technique: Red Canary researchers demonstrate using cgroups (control groups) as forensic artifacts to track malicious processes and container escapes on compromised servers.
Key findings: • Cgroups expose systemd service names, user IDs, login sessions, and container/pod IDs in structured paths like /user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-10.scope • Attackers cannot easily evade cgroups since they're kernel-enforced for resource management in systemd and containerized environments • Technique helped identify container-to-host escape: malicious activity progressed from Docker containers (5c2c04, ef4b8f) to host system user session • Data collection via /proc/$PID/cgroup, /sys/fs/cgroup, or EDR tools like Falco with custom YAML config
Detection opportunities: • Anomaly detection for unexpected services (apache.service appearing on nginx-only cluster) • Process grouping by cgroup paths to correlate related malicious activities • Enhanced context for credential searching, reconnaissance, and lateral movement alerts
Collect cgroups via inode monitoring or eBPF bpf_get_current_cgroup_id(). Layer onto existing detections for improved fidelity and attack timeline reconstruction.

item.title: Another Crack in the Chain of Trust: Uncovering (Yet Another) Secure Boot Bypass
item.description:
Binarly Research exposes CVE-2025-3052 (BRLY-2025-001): memory corruption in Microsoft-signed UEFI module enables arbitrary memory writes and complete Secure Boot bypass on most UEFI systems.
Critical technical details: • Affects 14 modules signed with "Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011" certificate - same cert used for Linux shim bootloader • Root cause: unsafe handling of IhisiParamBuffer NVRAM variable allows arbitrary memory write primitive • Attack overwrites gSecurity2 global variable to disable Secure Boot enforcement during boot process • Originally DT Research BIOS flashing tool (Dtbios-efi64-71.22.efi), signed October 2022, discovered on VirusTotal November 2024 • Insyde-based devices protected due to variable locking, but all other UEFI systems vulnerable
Attack methodology: • Privileged attacker sets malicious IhisiParamBuffer value from OS • Registers vulnerable module + unsigned payload module in UEFI Boot Manager • On reboot, vulnerable module executes during BDS phase, overwrites security checks • Unsigned payload executes with Secure Boot appearing enabled to OS
Impact enables bootkit installation before OS loads, bypassing all OS-level defenses. Microsoft added 14 hashes to Secure Boot dbx on June 10, 2025 Patch Tuesday.
Update Secure Boot dbx immediately. Hunt for unexpected UEFI modules in Boot Manager and monitor NVRAM variable modifications.
